findings.summary: The Concurrency vs Parallelism table's 'Tools' row packs several ideas into one cell.
findings.evidence: processes; threads only in GIL-releasing C or free-threaded builds
findings.fix: Split the cell into separate rows: processes always give parallelism, threads give parallelism only in GIL-releasing C code, threads give parallelism in free-threaded builds.

findings.summary: The decision rule is written as arrow-text lines, not as a diagram.
findings.evidence: What is the work waiting on? --waiting--> Network / disk (I/O-bound): threads or asyncio
findings.fix: Render it as a small two-branch flowchart or a two-row table: waiting (I/O-bound) goes to threads or asyncio, computing (CPU-bound) goes to processes.

findings.summary: Code appears before the idea it illustrates, and the producer/consumer example does not show a CPU-bound counterpart.
findings.evidence: queue.Queue is the thread-safe producer to consumer handoff ... then the python block
findings.fix: State the one-line idea (producer puts, consumer gets, join waits) immediately before each code block, then show the code.

findings.summary: A bullet holds multiple ideas and the 'CPU-bound code' callout is a prose sentence packing three claims.
findings.evidence: Threads give no speedup under the GIL, and lock contention plus switching can make them slower.
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: no speedup under the GIL; lock contention and switching can make threads slower.

findings.summary: The pickling flow is listed as separate fragments rather than a followable diagram, and its steps read as an unlinked list.
findings.evidence:
Pickle args
parent
Unpickle
worker
Run fn
own GIL
Pickle result
back to parent
findings.fix: Draw it as a single left-to-right flow: parent pickles args -> worker unpickles -> runs fn (own GIL) -> pickles result -> parent unpickles.

findings.summary: The 'Missing guard' callout is a prose sentence chaining several ideas and repeats earlier content; the spawn bullet also holds several ideas.
findings.evidence: Without the __main__ guard, spawn re-runs top-level code in every child, which stops with RuntimeError, so no work gets done.
findings.fix: Use short bullets: spawn re-imports the module; unguarded start call runs in each child; child raises RuntimeError.

findings.summary: The communication tools table appears under 'Data Between Processes' with no stated idea before it, and Queue/Pipe/shared_memory are not named as the alternative to pickling.
findings.evidence:
Tool | Use for
Queue | many producers and consumers
findings.fix: Add a one-line lead-in such as 'Other ways to move data between processes' above the table.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "executor.map").
findings.evidence: `executor.map(fn, items)` returns results in input order and raises the first exception when you iterate over it
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The Getting Results table cells mix several ideas and the 'Error raised' column is hard to follow.
findings.evidence: map(fn, items) | results | input order | first one, while iterating
findings.fix: Reword the column to 'When errors surface' with entries like 'submit: at result(); map: when iterating to the failing item; as_completed: at result()'.

findings.summary: The first bullet of Coroutines and Awaiting holds two ideas, and the free-threading bullet crams several facts together.
findings.evidence: Calling async def only makes a coroutine object; it runs when awaited or scheduled
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: calling async def returns a coroutine object; it runs only when awaited or scheduled. Split the free-threaded bullet into what it is, and its caveats.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet's picker does not mention threads versus Pool tool names consistently ('Pool' vs 'ProcessPoolExecutor') and the rule of thumb is a prose run-on.
findings.evidence: Measure first. Threads for I/O, processes for CPU, asyncio for thousands of connections. Free-threaded only after library support is confirmed.
findings.fix: Turn the rule of thumb into four one-line bullets and use the same tool names as the picker table.
